question: A team member is struggling with a task. What would usually NOT happen?
options: They raise it at the daily scrum as soon as they realise there is a problem
The sprint is lengthened by a couple of days to give them more time
Teammates with capacity chip in to help them get the task finished
The Scrum Master works to remove impediments and get the right support

question: When should blockers be raised?
options: At the sprint retrospective, once the sprint has ended
As early as possible, such as at the next daily scrum
At the next sprint planning meeting
At the sprint review, so the stakeholders hear about them

question: During sprint planning, how should a team decide how much to take on?
options: Whatever the product owner asks for, because the product owner knows the product best
Realistically, based on the story points it can handle, so that the sprint is sustainable
As much as possible, so that the product goal is reached sooner than the stakeholders expect
The same number of items as the previous sprint, regardless of how big each item is

question: Which of these is NOT something that Scrum says about the Scrum Master?
options: They coach the team in following the framework
They help remove impediments for the team
They facilitate the Scrum meetings
They act as the boss and tell people what to do

question: The mood-tracking retrospective board with sticky notes (cliffs and valleys) was described as suited to which point?
options: A final retrospective, looking back over all of the sprints
Sprint planning, to decide how many story points the team can take on
Requirements gathering, to rank the stakeholders by power and interest
The daily scrum, to track each person's blockers every morning

question: What are requirements for a software project?
options: The documentation produced after the software has been delivered, to describe how it works
The list of meetings the team must hold during each sprint, and the order in which they happen
The roles that the Scrum team needs to fill, and the responsibilities of each person in it
The tasks and conditions that must be met for the project to finish successfully, including what the software should do

question: Which groups use requirements?
options: Only the stakeholders who pay for the project
Only developers and testers
Only the product owner and the Scrum Master
Business and stakeholders, developers and testers

question: Why do developers and testers each need the requirements?
options: Both only need them to estimate the effort in story points
Developers need to know what to test; testers need to know what to develop
Developers need to know what to develop; testers need to know what to test
Neither needs them once the user stories are written

question: Which statement correctly distinguishes functional from non-functional requirements?
options: Functional requirements are written by developers; non-functional requirements are written by stakeholders
Non-functional requirements describe what the system does in response to actions; functional requirements describe qualities such as performance, security and reliability
Functional requirements must be done first; non-functional requirements can be dropped if there is no time
Functional requirements describe what the system does in response to actions; non-functional requirements describe qualities such as performance, security and reliability

question: A student suggests non-functional requirements can be left behind when time is short, since functional ones are the essentials. What is the correct view?
options: It is wrong; non-functional requirements are always higher priority than functional ones
That is correct; functional requirements are never negotiable and non-functional ones are always optional
That is correct; non-functional requirements are always lower priority
Priority is a separate matter; both functional and non-functional requirements can be high or low priority

question: 'When I log in, I should see my customer portal.' How is this requirement best classified?
options: Non-functional (security)
Functional
Non-functional (usability)
Non-functional (performance)

question: 'When I add an item to my basket, the total cost and item count should update immediately.' How is this requirement best classified?
options: Non-functional (legal and compliance)
Non-functional (maintainability)
Non-functional (scalability)
Functional

question: 'The system should process transactions within two seconds under normal load conditions.' Which category does this fall under?
options: Non-functional: reliability
Non-functional: performance
Functional: transactions
Non-functional: scalability

question: Why was the two-second transaction requirement described as a bit vague?
options: Two seconds is always impossible to achieve, so the requirement can never be met in practice
It does not state how many users are logged in, and the product owner has not agreed it
Transactions are only a functional requirement, so a time limit cannot be set on them at all
It does not say which transaction, and some, such as a payment, take longer without the system being slow

question: 'The system should meet the AA standard of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines.' Which non-functional category is this?
options: Legal and compliance
Accessibility
Maintainability
Usability

question: Which category describes the ability to add more users without breaking the system, with extra resources spinning up when needed?
options: Performance
Maintainability
Reliability
Scalability

question: Which category covers a certain amount of uptime and the system being highly available?
options: Scalability
Legal and compliance
Usability
Reliability

question: Which category covers how easily the system can be kept up to date, including the way the code is written and the architecture is structured?
options: Accessibility
Usability
Scalability
Maintainability

question: Which category covers how data is handled and where it is allowed to be stored, sometimes requiring redundancy?
options: Reliability
Maintainability
Security
Legal and compliance

question: Which non-functional categories are DevOps engineers often more responsible for implementing?
options: Maintainability and usability only
Usability, accessibility, maintainability and legal
Performance, security, reliability and scalability
Usability and accessibility only

question: Which category pairing is more often thought of by front-end and UX designers than by DevOps engineers?
options: Reliability and legal compliance
Security and scalability
Performance and reliability
Usability and accessibility

question: Which of these is NOT a technique for gathering requirements mentioned in the training?
options: Drawing a burn down chart
Observation of current workflows
Document analysis
Workshops

question: A team watches how staff currently carry out a process and reads the existing documentation to see what could be improved. Which technique is this?
options: Observation, together with document analysis
Prototyping, together with surveys
Workshops, together with questionnaires
Brainstorming, together with interviews

question: A team shows stakeholders a quick preliminary mock-up, gathers feedback, and tries another version until it fits what they want. Which technique is this?
options: Prototyping
Document analysis
Surveys and questionnaires
Competitor analysis

question: A team gets people from one department together to map out what they do when certain things happen, to build requirements from that. Which technique is this?
options: Questionnaires
Interviews
Prototyping
Workshops

question: What advantage do interviews have over surveys when gathering requirements?
options: You can reach far more people for the same amount of effort and cost as a survey
They produce statistics that can be used straight away without needing any analysis
You can ask additional questions if you do not get the information you need
They need no preparation, because the questions come up naturally during the conversation

question: A team looks at what competitors already offer, to find what they are missing and what could be provided differently. Which technique is this?
options: Brainstorming
Competitor analysis
Observation
Prototyping

question: Which is the correct structure of a user story?
options: As a [type of user], I want [a goal], so that [a reason]
Given [a context], when [an action], then [an outcome]
I want [a goal], as a [reason], so that [type of user]
As a [goal], I want [type of user], so that [a reason]

question: Which is a correctly written user story?
options: As an instructor, I want to see the bookings for the day, so that I can plan my lessons
I want a booking page that lists the bookings for each day so lessons can be planned
As an instructor, the system should list the bookings for the day when I log in
Given I am an instructor, when I log in, then I should see the list of bookings for the day

question: Is the 'so that' part of a user story compulsory?
options: Yes, a user story without it is invalid and cannot be used
No, but it is often very helpful, so use your judgement
Yes, but only for epics, where the reason needs to be explained
No, and it should always be left out to keep the story short

question: What is a user story's level of detail meant to be at first?
options: A full specification, written completely before the project starts and then locked
A legally binding contract with the exact wording agreed by the stakeholders
A pointer, with the detail fleshed out later and iteratively as development gets closer
A complete technical design, with every detail ready for the developers to code from

question: What does it mean that a user story card is 'a promise of a future conversation'?
options: The card does not hold everything; the conversation later fleshes out the requirements
The developers promise to finish the story in the sprint
The stakeholders promise to approve the story at the sprint review
The product owner promises not to change the story once it is written

question: In the secure login example, which of these is the user story that sits under the epic?
options: Secure login for the whole of the customer portal
Passwords must be hashed before they are stored in the database
Sprint 1 will deliver the secure login feature to the stakeholders
As a customer, I need a link so I can reset my password

question: In the same example, what does 'secure login' represent?
options: A single user story, written for the login page only
The bigger feature, which is broken down into user stories
The sprint goal for the first sprint of the project
An acceptance criterion for the registration form

question: What is an epic?
options: A type of meeting held at the end of a sprint
A bug that cannot be fixed in one sprint
An umbrella for a group of related user stories
A single small user story ready for a sprint

question: Who can write user stories?
options: Only the stakeholders, who understand the business need
Only the Scrum Master, who facilitates the Scrum processes
Only the product owner, who is responsible for the backlog
Anyone on the team, and everyone should contribute

question: Why should everyone on a Scrum team contribute user stories?
options: It reduces the number of stories that the product owner has to read and prioritise each sprint
It means that the Scrum Master never has to review the product backlog before a sprint starts
It means that only the developers' stories are used, since they know the product best
People have different opinions and expertise, and one person alone may not realise a story is needed

question: Who is responsible for ordering the user stories in the product backlog?
options: Whoever wrote each story, so that authors can protect their ideas
The product owner, who has the best understanding of the product
The Scrum Master, based on how the team is feeling in the sprint
The stakeholder who is paying for the work, as they know their needs

question: Who are the Three Amigos?
options: A business person (such as the product owner), a tester and a developer
The product owner, the Scrum Master and a developer working together
A developer, a tester and a DevOps engineer from the platform team
The product owner, the Scrum Master and a tester from the test team

question: Why is the tester one of the Three Amigos?
options: To write the code for the story while the business person and the developer talk it through
To ask how a requirement can be tested; if no test can be written, the story is not well written
To decide the priority of the story and where it should sit in the product backlog
To approve the budget for the story and check that it can be afforded in the sprint

question: What does INVEST stand for?
options: Integrated, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Tested
Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable
Independent, Necessary, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable
Independent, Negotiable, Verifiable, Estimable, Sizeable, Testable

question: Story B cannot be built until story A is done. Which INVEST letter is this breaking?
options: Negotiable
Estimable
Small
Independent

question: Which user story is more negotiable?
options: As a driver, I want a red Porsche 911 with leather seats
As a driver, I want a car
As a driver, I want a Porsche 911
As a driver, I want a Porsche 911 delivered on Friday

question: A developer proposes a feature that would be 'awesome' but does not fit what the product needs to do. Which INVEST letter is this breaking?
options: Independent
Valuable
Testable
Estimable

question: A story is too big to say how long it will take. What does this suggest, and which INVEST letters are affected?
options: It is a sprint goal, and it is not Independent
It may really be an epic, and it is not Estimable or Small
It is an acceptance criterion, and it is not Testable
It is a feature, and it is not Valuable

question: The tester cannot see how to write a test for a story. Which INVEST letter is this breaking?
options: Negotiable
Testable
Valuable
Independent

question: What are the 3 C's of a user story?
options: Customer, Conversation, Confirmation
Card, Conversation, Confirmation
Card, Collaboration, Confirmation
Card, Conversation, Completion

question: In the Card, Conversation, Confirmation model, which C is the acceptance criteria and tests that show the story is done?
options: Card
Confirmation
Completion
Conversation

question: A user story should be understandable by whom?
options: Only the tester who will write tests from it, as they are the specialist
Only the developers who will build it and understand the technical terms
People generally, without needing to be a technical specialist
Only the product owner who wrote it, since it is a note for their own use

question: When the instructor allowed AI to help with user stories and acceptance criteria, what was the condition?
options: AI may only be used after the product owner has approved the output in the sprint review
AI can only be used for estimating story points, not for writing the stories or the criteria
The output must be reviewed, because it may not be how you want the product to work
The output can be accepted as it is, since AI-written stories are accurate and consistent
